transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Lead Infra Eng, Aurelius), Marcus Hale (Platform SRE, Aurelius), Sofia Chen (Security Architect, Aurelius)

Summary:
High-level private VPC deep dive focused on networking patterns (PrivateLink vs VPC peering, NAT/EGRESS, subnets, DNS), plus runtime performance considerations (latency/throughput, KV cache, batching, quantization) for Aurelius's mixed latency/throughput workload (inference for chat + batch embeddings). Action items captured at end.

Topics:
- PrivateLink / endpoints vs peering
- NAT and egress strategies for model downloads and telemetry
- Subnet sizing and placement for GPU hosts
- DNS resolution, private hosted zones, and split-horizon needs
- Runtime: continuous batching, KV cache warmup, quantization tradeoffs
- Security: KMS, mutual TLS, audit logs, SOC 2 considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: alright, uh hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, i think we have the right folks on the call?
[00:12] Lena: yeah thanks, lena here, i, we run the platform infra at Aurelius so this is mostly on our side about networking and security constraints.
[00:20] Marcus: Marcus, platform SRE. main questions are egress costs and how the runtime behaves across private links.
[00:30] Priya: hi all, i'm Priya, i'll do the SE parts - we'll walk through our recommended VPC topology and then dive into runtime perf tradeoffs.
[00:37] Sofia: Sofia, security. i want details around KMS, audit logs, and whether any control-plane traffic hits the public internet.

[02:05] Priya: high-level, Redwood Private runs a small control plane in our managed region, but for the VPC deployment the inference nodes (gpu hosts) sit in your VPC. we support two networking models: PrivateLink (AWS ENIs / interface endpoints) and VPC peering/direct connect for other clouds. PrivateLink is the path we recommend when you want strict isolation — it leaves the control plane in our account but the data plane never routes over public subnets.
[02:45] Marcus: ok, can you explain what flows over PrivateLink? is model payload data streaming over that endpoint?
[02:52] Priya: yes so inference request / response traffic between your app and our runtime goes over the interface endpoint. model artifacts downloads (e.g. when provisioning a model the first time) can be configured to pull from an S3 bucket in your account via VPC endpoints, or we can ship a preloaded image. we usually recommend customers host model weights in their private S3 and we pull over VPC endpoints to avoid public egress.
[03:30] Lena: what about egress for container updates and telemetry? we want minimal north-south.
[03:36] Jordan: telemetry and metrics can be routed through your NAT or through a dedicated telemetry endpoint; for compliance customers we provide an option to buffer telemetry locally and ship via your proxy. default hosted telemetry hits our managed control plane, but that's opt-in to central telemetry.

[05:10] Priya: subnet sizing: for GPU nodes we suggest dedicated private subnets in at least two AZs. keep /24-ish subnets per AZ if you plan to scale to dozens of hosts; each gpu host needs an IP for the host and optionally for sidecars or ENIs if using PrivateLink. also keep an additional pool for autoscaling network interfaces.
[05:45] Marcus: and IP exhaustion is a real concern for us, so we might prefer smaller instance counts per subnet. does Redwood support secondary ENIs?
[05:55] Priya: yep we support secondary ENIs and placement constraints. in practice if you have strict IP limits we recommend using fewer but larger subnets or using a NAT Gateway with SNAT for outbound only.

[07:20] Lena: DNS — we use Route53 private hosted zones with split-horizon for internal names. how will Redwood's endpoints resolve?
[07:28] Priya: with PrivateLink we create interface endpoints that have IPs in your subnets so DNS is local. we provide CNAMEs and recommend adding private hosted zone records to map friendly names (eg redwood-inference.local) to the endpoint. for peering, you can use cross-account hosted zones or conditional forwarding.
[07:55] Sofia: any gotchas with TLS termination? do we need to manage certs on our side?
[08:00] Priya: TLS is mutual on the control plane for customer-managed deployments. Data plane TLS is terminated at the inference host, and for PrivateLink the interface endpoint is inside your VPC so your traffic never leaves. we integrate with your KMS for model encryption at rest if you want us to.

[09:40] Jordan: switching to runtime perf, Priya — can you cover KV cache and batching behavior with long context chat workloads?
[09:48] Priya: sure. Redwood runtime does continuous batching and KV cache management to optimize throughput. for chat workloads with long histories we use prefix caching and a per-client KV cache to avoid re-encoding the entire context. warmup is important — first requests will populate the cache so you'll see higher latency for cold sessions. Typical pattern: after warmup we can achieve 2-4x throughput improvement for repeated contexts, depending on model and quantization.
[10:30] Marcus: what's the effect on tail latency when batching is aggressive? we have 99th percentile SLOs.
[10:38] Priya: batching increases token-level throughput but adds queuing latency. you can set a latency SLO that primes a max batch delay (e.g., 10–50ms). Redwood's scheduler supports latency buckets: latency-first (small batches), throughput-first (larger batches), or hybrid. For 99th p you can pin to a small max-batch-delay and enable KV caching to recover throughput.

[12:05] Lena: quantization — we have concerns about hallucinations and quality with 4-bit quantization. what's Redwood's guidance?
[12:12] Priya: quantization is model dependent. we provide quantization profiles validated per model. For generative chat we generally recommend 8-bit q4_0 for production to balance quality and speed; 4-bit can work for embeddings or non-critical passes. We also support mixed-precision where attention layers remain higher precision. We'll run benchmark comparisons for your specific prompts as part of the pilot.

[13:50] Marcus: are there runtime differences when using quantized models in terms of memory and KV cache mechanics?
[13:57] Priya: quantized weights reduce memory footprint so you can pack more models per host, but KV cache size is dominated by sequence length and hidden-size, which doesn't shrink with weight quantization. so the memory benefit is mostly for weights, not the runtime caches. batching and KV cache eviction policies behave the same.

[15:30] Sofia: security — do we get audit logs for each inference request? we need request-level tracing and immutable logs for SOC2.
[15:38] Jordan: yes, Redwood Private can ship request-level metadata to your logging endpoint; payloads are not stored unless you enable retention for debugging. audit logs (control plane actions, onboarding, rollouts) are retained and can be exported to your S3 or your SIEM over a private endpoint.

[17:10] Priya: one common implementation detail: model artifact downloads. if you keep artifacts in your account's S3 we suggest an interface endpoint to avoid public egress; if you prefer Redwood-hosted artifacts we can provide signing and put the object in a customer-scoped bucket for the initial provisioning.

[19:00] Marcus: network policy question — do hosts need outbound internet access for health checks or licensing?
[19:06] Priya: no outbound to public internet required for normal inference. optional components like kernel updates or image pulls can be handled via an internal image registry or by pre-baking images. health checks between control and data plane go over the PrivateLink.

[21:15] Lena: what about cross-region failover? we do active-active between us-east-1 and us-west-2. how does Redwood handle cross-region model synchronization?
[21:22] Priya: we support async replication of models to multiple regions; you'll want to push artifacts to each region's private S3 or have cross-region replication enabled. There is also an option for on-demand pull in a cold region but that impacts first-request latency.

[23:40] Marcus: performance numbers — can you give ballpark latencies for 2k and 4k token contexts on a T4/RTX size host?
[23:48] Priya: ballpark very roughly: on large-A100-class hosts for autoregressive models you might see ~70–120ms per token for 2k with batching, 150–220ms per token for large contexts without KV cache. On more commodity GPUs it's higher. But we emphasized numbers will vary - we'll run exact baselines with your workloads.

[25:10] Jordan: let's talk fallback and graceful degradation if capacity is constrained.
[25:18] Priya: Redwood routing supports model fallbacks and tiered capacity. If your primary heavy model is offline we can route to a compatible, smaller model; you can configure quality thresholds so you do not accept models below X accuracy. This is policy-driven in the console.

[27:00] Lena: do you support SRv6 / advanced overlay networking? we have a service mesh overlay internally.
[27:07] Priya: we can integrate; the data plane sits in your VPC so it sees your service mesh if you put it in front. There are caveats with container networking and kernel optimizations for high throughput — we'll share recommended CNI settings.

[29:40] Marcus: any special ports for PrivateLink setup we should pre-approve in our firewall?
[29:46] Priya: we compiled a checklist — by default you need outbound HTTPS (443) from the host for the interface endpoint management, and the PrivateLink endpoints open a set of ephemeral ports for the ENIs. we'll share the exact port list; also if you're using a hardware firewall we recommend allowing the Redwood control plane IP ranges for admin operations.

[31:10] Jordan: ok we should surface a list: port checklist, CIDRs, example CloudFormation/Terraform. Jordan will send a repo link.
[31:20] Lena: yep that would be helpful.

[33:00] Priya: one runtime note: when you use aggressive batching we recommend enabling conservative KV cache eviction to avoid spike mem usage. and set a max_context_size to prevent very long user sessions from blowing memory.

[35:10] Sofia: encryption keys — KMS integration: how does key rotation work?
[35:16] Priya: we integrate with your KMS; model snapshots are encrypted with your key. rotations are supported — we re-encrypt at rest as part of the rotation workflow. we keep key usage logs for audit.

[37:45] Marcus: telemetry volume — if we route metrics through our VPC what's the expected cardinality and bandwidth?
[37:52] Priya: typical telemetry is small (per-request metadata, counters), maybe a few KB per request. if you stream full traces or embeddings you'll see much higher volume. we can sample traces and push aggregated metrics to save bandwidth.

[40:00] Lena: can we do an internal perf pilot? spin up a small pool of GPU hosts in our VPC and run our chat workload with real traffic?
[40:07] Jordan: absolutely — our recommended pilot is a 3-node pool (two AZs) with 1–2 models loaded, run for 72 hrs with your load generator. Priya will help configure the batching/latency buckets and run baselines.

[42:20] Priya: I'll need a sample prompt set, token distribution, and an example embedding workload. Also the CIDR blocks and a test AWS account/role to provision the endpoints.

[44:10] Sofia: we'll also need to validate that control plane operations (rollouts) require RBAC and MFA.
[44:16] Jordan: yes RBAC in the console with SSO is supported; provisioning operations are tied to roles. We'll share our admin role mappings.

[46:30] Marcus: one more question — if we want to run on-prem later, is the networking model similar?
[46:38] Priya: on-prem is similar conceptually but you'd run the entire control plane and data plane in your network; we provide an appliance container set and a connector. Networking wise you control everything so PrivateLink is replaced by local endpoints; we still recommend isolated subnets for GPU hosts and an internal registry for images.

[49:00] Jordan: ok quick recap then next steps.
[49:06] Jordan: recap — Redwood Private supports PrivateLink or peering; inference hosts sit in your VPC; model artifacts can be pulled from your S3 via endpoints; KV cache and batching provide throughput gains after warmup; quantization is supported with profiles; KMS integration and audit logs are available. Pilot plan: 3-node pool, run 72 hrs, Redwood to provide network diagram, port list, and benchmark harness.

[51:30] Lena: that sounds good. please include any config examples (terraform) and the recommended CNIs.
[51:36] Priya: will do.

[52:10] Sofia: for security, please attach the SOC2 summary and our checklist mapping.
[52:15] Jordan: we'll send SOC2 and security whitepaper — Jordan to follow up.

[53:00] Marcus: timeline — can we get the pilot ready by week of 2026-01-25?
[53:06] Jordan: yes if we get CIDR and a test role by 2026-01-19 we can.

[54:30] Priya: i'll run the initial perf runs and share the spreadsheet by 2026-01-20.

[55:10] Jordan: great, thanks everyone. we'll send notes and links.
[55:16] Lena: thanks all.
[55:20] Sofia: thanks.
